title: Symmetric matrices (spectral theorem) & SVD
summary: Symmetric matrices are exactly the ones with an orthonormal eigenbasis (A = PDPᵀ), and every matrix, even rectangular, has a singular value decomposition A = UΣVᵀ built from the symmetric matrix AᵀA. The SVD exposes rank and orthonormal bases of all four fundamental subspaces.

lesson.title: Symmetric matrices and why they are special

blocks.text: A square matrix with Aᵀ = A (entries mirror across the diagonal).

blocks.name: Orthogonal eigenvectors
blocks.text: If A is symmetric, eigenvectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal.

proof.text: Let Av₁ = λ₁v₁, Av₂ = λ₂v₂, λ₁ ≠ λ₂. Then λ₁(v₁·v₂) = (Av₁)ᵀv₂ = v₁ᵀAᵀv₂ = v₁ᵀAv₂ = λ₂(v₁·v₂). So (λ₁ − λ₂)(v₁·v₂) = 0, forcing v₁·v₂ = 0. The only use of symmetry is Aᵀ = A.

blocks.name: Real eigenvalues
blocks.text: A real symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues.

proof.text: Suppose Av = λv with v ≠ 0 possibly complex. Then v̄ᵀAv = λv̄ᵀv = λ‖v‖². Take the conjugate transpose of the scalar v̄ᵀAv: since A is real and symmetric it equals itself, so it is real. Hence λ = (real)/(‖v‖² > 0) is real.

blocks.text: Inside ONE eigenspace (a repeated eigenvalue) a basis found by row reduction need not be orthogonal: you must run Gram–Schmidt there. Non-symmetric matrices like [1 1; 0 2] have non-orthogonal eigenvectors (1, 0), (1, 1).

Examples: [3 1; 1 3] and [5 2; 2 2] are symmetric; [1 1; 0 2] is not, and indeed its eigenvectors (1, 0) and (1, 1) are not orthogonal. AᵀA and AAᵀ are always symmetric (since (AᵀA)ᵀ = AᵀAᵀᵀ = AᵀA), which is why they appear in least squares and the SVD.

lesson.title: The Spectral Theorem and orthogonal diagonalization

blocks.text: A = PDPᵀ with P orthogonal (P⁻¹ = Pᵀ) and D diagonal.

blocks.name: Spectral Theorem
blocks.text: An n×n real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable ⇔ it is symmetric. For symmetric A: (a) n real eigenvalues counting multiplicity; (b) each eigenspace has dimension equal to the algebraic multiplicity; (c) eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal; (d) A = PDPᵀ.

proof.text: ⇐ direction (orthogonally diagonalizable ⇒ symmetric) is one line: (PDPᵀ)ᵀ = PDᵀPᵀ = PDPᵀ. The ⇒ direction uses the two theorems above plus an induction argument for (b).

blocks.title: Orthogonally diagonalize a symmetric A
items: Find a basis of each eigenspace.
Run Gram–Schmidt INSIDE each eigenspace of dimension ≥ 2 (different eigenspaces are already orthogonal).
Normalize every vector; P = [u₁ ⋯ uₙ], D = diag of the matching eigenvalues. Then A = PDPᵀ.

blocks.title: Orthogonal diagonalization with a repeated eigenvalue
steps: Gram–Schmidt in the eigenspace: (−1, 2, 0) − (−1/2)(1, 0, 1) = (−1/2, 2, 1/2) → (−1, 4, 1). Still an eigenvector (it is in the eigenspace).
λ = −2: A + 2I = [5 −2 4; −2 8 2; 4 2 5] → eigenvector (−2, −1, 2). Check it is orthogonal to both λ = 7 vectors: −2 + 0 + 2 = 0, 2 − 4 + 2 = 0. ✓

blocks.title: Orthogonally diagonalize a 2×2 (routine)
steps: Normalize: P = (1/√5)[2 −1; 1 2], D = diag(6, 1), A = PDPᵀ.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt inside a 2-dimensional eigenspace (exam-hard)
steps: Row sums are 0 ⇒ A(1, 1, 1) = 0: λ = 0 with eigenvector (1, 1, 1).
A − 3I = [−1 −1 −1; −1 −1 −1; −1 −1 −1], rank 1 ⇒ λ = 3 with eigenspace x₁ + x₂ + x₃ = 0, basis (−1, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 1) (dot product 1: not orthogonal).

blocks.name: Spectral decomposition
blocks.text: If A = PDPᵀ with orthonormal columns u₁, …, uₙ, then A = λ₁u₁u₁ᵀ + λ₂u₂u₂ᵀ + ⋯ + λₙuₙuₙᵀ. Each uⱼuⱼᵀ is the n×n rank-1 matrix of orthogonal projection onto Span{uⱼ}.

proof.text: Column-row expansion of the product: PDPᵀ = [λ₁u₁ ⋯ λₙuₙ][u₁ᵀ; …; uₙᵀ] = Σλⱼuⱼuⱼᵀ.

blocks.text: A acts by splitting a vector into its components along the orthonormal eigenvectors and scaling each by its eigenvalue. This also gives Aᵏ = Σλⱼᵏuⱼuⱼᵀ and A⁻¹ = Σλⱼ⁻¹uⱼuⱼᵀ.

blocks.title: Spectral decomposition of a 2×2
blocks.prompt: Write the spectral decomposition of A = [7 2; 2 4].

blocks.title: Powers from the spectral decomposition (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For A = [5 2; 2 2], write A = 6u₁u₁ᵀ + 1·u₂u₂ᵀ and use it to find the (1, 2) entry of A³.

blocks.text: u₁u₁ᵀ + u₂u₂ᵀ + ⋯ + uₙuₙᵀ = I (the projections onto an orthonormal basis add up to the identity). So for A = I + 9uuᵀ-type matrices, eigenvalue 1 sits on u⊥ and 10 on u.
Non-square or non-symmetric matrices have no orthogonal eigenbasis, but AᵀA is always symmetric. That is the door to the SVD.
Let λ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ λₙ be the eigenvalues of AᵀA with orthonormal eigenvectors v₁, …, vₙ. The singular values of A are σᵢ = √λᵢ = ‖Avᵢ‖.

blocks.name: Singular values are ≥ 0
blocks.text: Each eigenvalue of AᵀA satisfies λᵢ = ‖Avᵢ‖² ≥ 0, so σᵢ is a well-defined nonnegative number: the amount A stretches the unit vector vᵢ.

proof.text: ‖Avᵢ‖² = (Avᵢ)ᵀ(Avᵢ) = vᵢᵀAᵀAvᵢ = vᵢᵀ(λᵢvᵢ) = λᵢ (vᵢ is a unit vector).

blocks.name: SVD
blocks.text: Every m×n matrix of rank r factors as A = UΣVᵀ: V (n×n) and U (m×m) orthogonal, Σ m×n with σ₁ ≥ ⋯ ≥ σᵣ > 0 in the top-left diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The columns of V are right singular vectors, of U left singular vectors, and Avᵢ = σᵢuᵢ.

proof.text: {Av₁, …, Avᵣ} are orthogonal: (Avᵢ)·(Avⱼ) = vᵢᵀAᵀAvⱼ = λⱼ vᵢ·vⱼ = 0 for i ≠ j. Normalizing gives uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ; extend to an orthonormal basis of ℝᵐ. Then AV = UΣ, so A = UΣVᵀ.

blocks.title: SVD recipe
items: Compute AᵀA (n×n; for a wide matrix you may use AAᵀ instead, see below).
Its eigenvalues in decreasing order; σᵢ = √λᵢ. Number of nonzero σ's = rank.
If r < m, extend u₁, …, uᵣ to an orthonormal basis of ℝᵐ using Nul Aᵀ (Gram–Schmidt if needed) → U.
Σ has the same shape as A.

blocks.text: Do not compute U separately from eigenvectors of AAᵀ: signs may not match and A ≠ UΣVᵀ. Always use uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ.

blocks.title: SVD of a 2×3
blocks.prompt: Find the singular values and the SVD of A = [4 11 14; 8 7 −2].

blocks.text: For a wide matrix (m < n) it is often faster to work with the smaller matrix AAᵀ, whose nonzero eigenvalues are the same σᵢ², and then use vᵢ = Aᵀuᵢ/σᵢ.

blocks.title: SVD when AᵀA has a repeated eigenvalue (exam-hard twist)
steps: AᵀA = [2 0; 0 2] = 2I: every unit vector is an eigenvector, σ₁ = σ₂ = √2.
Any orthonormal V works; take V = I. Then uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ: u₁ = (1, −1)/√2, u₂ = (1, 1)/√2.
A = UΣVᵀ with U = (1/√2)[1 1; −1 1], Σ = √2·I, V = I. (A is √2 times a rotation, so it stretches every direction equally.)

blocks.text: Geometric meaning: A maps the unit circle (sphere) to an ellipse (ellipsoid). The right singular vectors vᵢ are the orthogonal directions that stay orthogonal after applying A; they land on the axes σᵢuᵢ of the ellipse. σ₁ is the longest semi-axis (the maximum stretch) and the smallest nonzero σ the shortest.

lesson.title: What the SVD tells you: rank and the four subspaces

blocks.name: Bases from the SVD
blocks.text: If A = UΣVᵀ has r nonzero singular values: rank A = r; {u₁, …, uᵣ} is an orthonormal basis of Col A; {uᵣ₊₁, …, uₘ} of Nul Aᵀ; {v₁, …, vᵣ} of Row A; {vᵣ₊₁, …, vₙ} of Nul A.

proof.text: Avᵢ = σᵢuᵢ ≠ 0 for i ≤ r and Avᵢ = 0 for i > r. So vᵣ₊₁, …, vₙ are n − r orthonormal vectors in Nul A, which has dimension n − r. The uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ span Col A. The rest follow from Row A = (Nul A)⊥ and Nul Aᵀ = (Col A)⊥.

blocks.title: Read off the subspaces
blocks.prompt: For A = [1 −1; −2 2; 2 −2] with the SVD above, give rank A and orthonormal bases of Col A, Nul A, Row A, Nul Aᵀ; and the maximum of ‖Ax‖ over unit x.
steps: max ‖Ax‖ = σ₁ = 3√2, attained at x = v₁.
blocks.answer: rank 1; Col: {u₁}; Nul Aᵀ: {u₂, u₃}; Row: {v₁}; Nul: {v₂}; max ‖Ax‖ = 3√2

items: Singular values ≠ eigenvalues in general ([0 1; 0 0]: eigenvalues 0, 0; singular values 1, 0). For symmetric A, σᵢ = |λᵢ|.
A and Aᵀ have the same nonzero singular values.
For square A, |det A| = σ₁σ₂⋯σₙ, and A is invertible iff all σᵢ > 0.
σ₁ = max ‖Ax‖ over unit x; σₙ (for n ≤ m) = min.

blocks.title: True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) Every symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. (b) The singular values of a square matrix are the absolute values of its eigenvalues. (c) The number of nonzero singular values equals rank A. (d) If A is orthogonally diagonalizable, A is symmetric. (e) Singular values can be negative.
steps: (b) False: [1 1; 0 1] has eigenvalues 1, 1 but singular values (√5 ± 1)/2. True only for symmetric (more generally normal) matrices.

blocks.title: Maximum and minimum stretch (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For A = [4 11 14; 8 7 −2] (σ₁ = 6√10, σ₂ = 3√10), find max ‖Ax‖ and min ‖Ax‖ over unit vectors x in ℝ³, and where they are attained.
steps: A is 2×3, so it has a nontrivial null space: min ‖Ax‖ = 0 at x = ±v₃ = ±(2, −2, 1)/3.
Restricted to Row A = Span{v₁, v₂}, the minimum would be σ₂ = 3√10.
blocks.answer: max 6√10 at v₁; min 0 at v₃

lesson.title: A complete SVD by hand: full rank 3×2

blocks.title: SVD of a 3×2 matrix with two nonzero singular values (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Find a full SVD of A = [3 2; 2 3; 2 −2] and orthonormal bases of the four fundamental subspaces.
steps: u₃ must be orthogonal to u₁ and u₂ (a basis of Nul Aᵀ): the cross product (1, 1, 0) × (1, −1, 4) = (4, −4, −2) gives u₃ = (2, −2, −1)/3.
Σ = [5 0; 0 3; 0 0]. Rank 2: Col A = Span{u₁, u₂}, Nul Aᵀ = Span{u₃}, Row A = ℝ² = Span{v₁, v₂}, Nul A = {0}.

blocks.text: Why uᵢ = Avᵢ/σᵢ is automatically a unit vector: ‖Avᵢ‖ = σᵢ (shown above). And why the uᵢ are orthogonal: (Avᵢ)·(Avⱼ) = vᵢᵀ(AᵀAvⱼ) = σⱼ²vᵢ·vⱼ = 0. These two facts are the entire proof of the SVD.

Keeping only the r nonzero singular values gives A = UᵣDᵣVᵣᵀ (Uᵣ is m×r, Dᵣ = diag(σ₁, …, σᵣ), Vᵣ is n×r). The pseudoinverse is A⁺ = VᵣDᵣ⁻¹Uᵣᵀ, and x̂ = A⁺b is the least-squares solution of minimum length.
Exam workflow: AᵀA → eigenvalues (sort decreasing) → σ = √λ → orthonormal v's → u = Av/σ → complete U with Nul Aᵀ. Check one entry of UΣVᵀ against A.

parsons.title: Symmetric ⇒ orthogonal eigenvectors
parsons.goal: Prove: if Aᵀ = A, Av₁ = λ₁v₁, Av₂ = λ₂v₂ and λ₁ ≠ λ₂, then v₁·v₂ = 0.
lines: Since Aᵀ = A, v₁ᵀAᵀv₂ = v₁ᵀ(Av₂) = v₁ᵀ(λ₂v₂) = λ₂(v₁·v₂).
distractors: Since A is invertible, v₁ᵀAᵀv₂ = v₁ᵀv₂.

parsons.title: Singular values are lengths
parsons.goal: Let v be a unit eigenvector of AᵀA with eigenvalue λ. Prove λ ≥ 0 and ‖Av‖ = √λ.
lines: Since AᵀAv = λv, vᵀAᵀAv = vᵀ(λv) = λ(vᵀv).
v is a unit vector, so vᵀv = 1 and ‖Av‖² = λ.
A squared length is ≥ 0, so λ ≥ 0 and ‖Av‖ = √λ = σ. ∎
distractors: v is an eigenvector, so ‖Av‖ = λ.

parsons.title: Orthogonally diagonalizable ⇒ symmetric
parsons.goal: Prove: if A = PDPᵀ with P orthogonal and D diagonal, then Aᵀ = A.
lines: (Pᵀ)ᵀ = P, and Dᵀ = D because D is diagonal.
distractors: Dᵀ = D⁻¹ because P is orthogonal.
